summary.title: Agentic World Modeling: Foundations, Capabilities, Laws, and Beyond

details: The term 'world model' means different things across RL, vision, NLP/agents, robotics, and AI-for-science, so papers claim progress under one interpretation while being incomparable under another; existing surveys organize by modality or application domain and thus miss the cross-modal capability progression.

A 'levels x laws' taxonomy: three capability levels (L1 Predictor = one-step local transition operators; L2 Simulator = multi-step action-conditioned rollouts respecting domain constraints; L3 Evolver = evidence-driven revision of the model itself) crossed with four governing-law regimes (physical, digital, social, scientific).

Each level boundary is given a POMDP-grounded formal definition with testable boundary conditions: L1->L2 requires long-horizon coherence, intervention sensitivity, and constraint consistency; L2->L3 requires evidence-grounded diagnosis, persistent asset update, and governed validation.
Levels are runtime capability stages an agent invokes (not disjoint model classes), and 'closed-loop use' is argued to be orthogonal to the level axis.

POMDP tuple (X, A, Omega, T, O, R, gamma) with learned latent state z_t; L1 factorized into four operators: inference q_phi(z_t|o_<=t,a_<=t-1), forward dynamics p_theta(z_t|z_{t-1},a_t), decoder p_psi(o_t|z_t), inverse dynamics pi_eta(a_t|z_{t-1},z_t).
L2 written as trajectory query p-hat(tau | z_0, a_{1:H}, c) with a governing-law compatibility factor phi_c(tau) over the whole rollout, so the distribution does not factorize per step.
L3 written as a design-execute-observe-reflect loop (M_t, d_t) -> M_{t+1} over the world-model stack.

Over 400 works reviewed, with 100+ representative systems tabulated across model-based RL (Dreamer family, MuZero, EfficientZero, TD-MPC2, IRIS, DIAMOND), video/interactive generation (Sora, Genie, GAIA-1, Oasis, MineWorld), web/GUI/tool agents (WebDreamer, DreamGym, WebWorld, MobileDreamer, GTM, SWE-World), social simulation (Generative Agents, Sotopia, CICERO, OASIS), and AI-for-science surrogates (GraphCast, GenCast, FNO, AlphaFold lineage, AI Scientist-v2, FunSearch/AlphaEvolve).

Physical: analytic/simulator-verifiable constraints (contact, gravity, kinematics); Digital: deterministic, mechanically verifiable program semantics; Social: opaque, reflexive, normative belief/commitment dynamics; Scientific: latent mechanisms only validatable against empirical measurement.
Regimes positioned along formalizability and observability of constraints; cross-regime examples (driving, Minecraft/Voyager, Diplomacy, autonomous labs) require joint constraint satisfaction.
Philosophical scaffolding maps levels to Hume's constant conjunction (L1), Lewis's closest possible worlds (L2), and Lakatos hard core/protective belt plus Duhem-Quine holism (L3).

Decision-centric evaluation principles, a minimal reproducible evaluation package, architectural/implementation guidance, historical timeline of four eras, and open problems including 'meta-world modeling' where governing laws themselves become learnable.
Explicitly not a new benchmark or leaderboard; positioned against prior surveys (Ding et al., Sora survey, G1-G4 visual roadmap, domain-specific surveys) on scope x organizing-principle axes.

key_findings.finding: A capability-based L1/L2/L3 hierarchy with testable boundary conditions provides a cross-modal coordinate system that modality- or domain-partitioned surveys cannot express.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines each level over a shared POMDP factorization, specifies three falsifiable boundary conditions per transition, and uses them to reclassify 100+ systems; it contrasts this with prior taxonomies (e.g., the visual G1-G4 roadmap) whose levels are tied to the visual modality and appearance-based interactivity.

key_findings.finding: The L1->L2 distinction is rollout fidelity under composition, not one-step accuracy, and requires a trajectory-level constraint term that breaks per-step factorization.
key_findings.evidence: Formally, L1 composition gives prod_t p_theta(z_t|z_{t-1},a_t) whereas L2 adds a governing-law compatibility factor phi_c(tau) over the whole rollout; the paper argues long-horizon coherence, intervention sensitivity, and constraint consistency are mutually non-implying and can trade off (e.g., aggressive constraint enforcement stabilizes trajectories but reduces intervention responsiveness).

key_findings.finding: L3 (evidence-driven revision of the model itself) is argued to be a qualitatively distinct capability rather than a deployment property of L2, and is realized only unevenly across domains.
key_findings.evidence: L2->L3 is separated by active information expansion, autonomous execution/observation, and belief revision with persistent, regression-gated asset updates; case analysis shows FunSearch/AlphaEvolve and AI Scientist-v2 implement only parts of the design-execute-observe-reflect loop (automated evaluators without persistent model revision or with revision targeting paper quality rather than mechanism), while robotics examples (self-modeling, AdaptSim) and autonomous labs supply the clearest instances.

key_findings.finding: Decision-usability, not perceptual fidelity, should govern world-model evaluation: 'a good simulator must look more like the constraints, not more like the world'.
key_findings.evidence: Cross-regime analysis identifies five recurring L2 failure modes (compounding error, state aliasing/drift, controllability failure, simulator escape/exploitability, calibration failure under shift) and notes that FVD-style distributional realism fails to capture controllability or constraint validity, motivating VBench-2.0-style physics/commonsense checks and explicit loggable, replayable, regressable constraints.

key_findings.finding: Representation choice is treated as constitutive rather than incidental: latent dynamics suffice as scaffolding for L1/L2 but genuine L3 law revision plausibly requires a symbolic substrate.
key_findings.evidence: The argument contrasts implicitly encoded invariances in neural architectures (translation equivariance, shape bias) with explicitly revisable symbolic theories (Newtonian to Lorentz invariance shift), and notes that structural edits to learned models do not predictably change captured invariances, whereas code/program world models (WorldCoder, CodeWM, Code World Models for games) expose transitions as inspectable, verifiable objects.
